title: India's EB-5 Filings Surge 25-Fold, Reshaping the U.S. Investor Green Card Landscape
excerpt: From 75 applications in fiscal 2022 to nearly 1,900 in fiscal 2025, Indian professionals are flooding the EB-5 program as H-1B backlogs deepen and a September 30 filing deadline looms
body:
• Indian EB-5 filings grew roughly 25-fold in three years — from about 75 in fiscal year 2022 to nearly 1,900 in fiscal year 2025, according to IIUSA data cited by The American Bazaar.
  • India now accounts for 22% of all EB-5 petitions filed worldwide since April 2022, second only to China, with over 3,000 total petitions through FY2025.
  • Most new Indian EB-5 investors are H-1B or F-1 visa holders seeking escape from employment-based green card backlogs exceeding 15 years.
  • A grandfathering deadline on September 30, 2026 is driving a final rush of filings before investment thresholds rise and current program rules potentially expire.

The U.S. EB-5 immigrant investor program, long dominated by Chinese applicants, is undergoing a rapid demographic shift. Indian nationals now represent the fastest-growing segment of the program's applicant pool, with filings increasing at a pace that immigration attorneys and industry groups say is unprecedented.

According to IIUSA data cited by The American Bazaar, EB-5 filings from India grew roughly 25-fold in three years, climbing from about 75 in fiscal year 2022 to nearly 1,900 in fiscal year 2025. Separate FOIA data analyzed by VisaVerge shows Indian EB-5 petitions reaching over 3,000 in FY2025, up from 1,200 in FY2023 — an increase that has made India the second-largest source market behind China.

H-1B Frustrations Fuel the Shift

The surge is driven less by newly wealthy Indians abroad than by professionals already living in the United States on temporary work visas. H-1B holders and F-1 graduates facing EB-2 green card backlogs exceeding 15 years for Indian nationals have turned to the EB-5 program's $800,000 minimum investment as a faster — if more expensive — alternative.

https://x.com/20kInvestor/status/2089179404643746066

"Most new EB-5 investors are H-1B or F-1 visa holders, mostly from India, and for them the real pain point is time, not price. Indian nationals filing through the standard employment-based categories are currently facing decades-long wait times because of per-country backlogs."

— Chaitrali Karve, Senior Director, LCR Capital Partners

Victor Espinosa, Vice President at Peachtree Group and a former Goldman Sachs wealth advisor, told The American Bazaar that Indian investors bring an "institutional-grade" approach to EB-5. "They are not simply immigrating; they are reallocating capital within a country where they already live and work," he said, noting that many evaluate projects with the rigor of private equity investors — scrutinizing capital stack positioning, developer track records, and exit assumptions.

The Numbers Behind the Shift

Newly released USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 shows the EB-5 program injected approximately $5.35 billion into the U.S. economy. A total of 6,307 investors filed petitions through Regional Centers, up sharply from 4,567 the prior year.

China still leads overall filings with 3,017 Regional Center petitions in FY2025, compared to India's 1,812, according to IMI Daily's analysis of the USCIS data. But the trajectory tells a different story. India's share of total EB-5 petitions filed since the 2022 reform now stands at 22% of 13,520 worldwide filings, per FOIA data. Five years ago, Indian investors accounted for just 4% of EB-5 filings.

Indian applicants have shown a clear preference for Targeted Employment Areas, with 847 petitions in rural TEA projects and 568 in high-unemployment areas through January 2025. Rural projects carry a 96% approval rate under the post-reform system, while high-unemployment area projects have a 93% approval rate — both far above the 30% denial rate plaguing legacy pre-reform petitions.

Retrogression Warning Complicates the Picture

The rapid growth has not come without consequences. The U.S. Department of State's May 2026 Visa Bulletin warned that Indian demand in the EB-5 unreserved category could force retrogression — or even temporary visa unavailability — before the fiscal year ends on September 30.

India's Final Action Date in EB-5 unreserved now stands at May 1, 2022, a cutoff that signals the category is already oversubscribed for Indian applicants. Reserved categories — rural, high-unemployment, and infrastructure — remain current for India, but experts warn that window could narrow.

Charlie Oppenheim, former Chief of the Visa Office at the U.S. Department of State, has cautioned that backlogs could form within reserved categories as well. "If demand from Indian nationals continues at this pace, we could see EB-5 backlogs form within reserved categories — just like they did in EB-2," he said.

The September 30 Deadline

Layered on top of the retrogression risk is a statutory deadline that immigration attorneys say is creating genuine urgency. Investors who file their I-526E petition on or before September 30, 2026, lock in the current EB-5 framework under a grandfathering provision in the Reform and Integrity Act of 2022. After that date, applicants face potential exposure to program changes if the Regional Center authorization lapses, and an inflation-adjusted investment minimum — projected to rise to $900,000–$975,000 for TEA projects — takes effect on January 1, 2027.

"A price increase is a number. A missed deadline is a plan that has to be rebuilt," Karve told The American Bazaar, noting that for families already navigating visa expirations and child aging-out risks, the calendar matters more than the dollar figure.

For Indian professionals who have spent years in the H-1B queue, the calculus has shifted. What was once a niche program for ultra-wealthy foreign investors has become a mainstream green card strategy — one now reshaping both the EB-5 industry and the broader immigration landscape.
nri_angle: Indian professionals on H-1B and F-1 visas in the U.S. are increasingly turning to the EB-5 investor visa as a green card alternative, driven by employment-based backlogs exceeding 15 years. The 25-fold surge in Indian EB-5 filings reflects a fundamental shift in how the diaspora approaches immigration strategy — from waiting in line to investing their way forward.
author: Diaspora Desk
